what_its_for: Ranibizumab-eqrn is used to treat certain eye conditions that can cause vision loss. These include wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), a type of swelling in the eye called macular edema (which can happen after a blood vessel blockage in the eye or in people with diabetes), and abnormal blood vessel growth under the retina caused by a condition called pathologic myopia (very severe nearsightedness). This medicine works by blocking a protein that causes abnormal, leaky blood vessels to grow in the eye.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an injection directly into your eye by your eye doctor (ophthalmologist) in a medical office or clinic. You will NOT give this injection to yourself at home. Before the injection, your doctor will clean your eye and use numbing drops so you feel as little discomfort as possible. The procedure is quick, usually taking only a few minutes. You may feel some pressure or mild discomfort during the injection. It is very important to keep all of your scheduled appointments so you receive your treatments on time.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the exact dose and how often you receive injections based on your specific eye condition. Typically, injections are given once a month (every 4 weeks). After the first several monthly injections, your doctor may change how often you come in based on how well your eye is responding to treatment. Never try to change your dosing schedule on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule an injection appointment, call your doctor's office as soon as possible to set up a new appointment. Try not to go too long between treatments, as skipping doses may allow your eye condition to worsen and could lead to more vision loss. Do not try to make up for a missed dose by getting two injections close together.
storage: You will not be storing this medication at home, as it is prepared and given by your eye doctor. If for any reason you are given information about storage, keep the medicine refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in the original packaging and protect it from light. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: After your injection, try to avoid rubbing or touching your eye, as this could cause an infection or injury. Avoid swimming pools, hot tubs, or getting water in your eye for at least 48 hours after each injection unless your doctor says otherwise. Do not wear contact lenses if your doctor has told you not to after your procedure. Let your doctor know about all other eye drops or medicines you are using, including over-the-counter products, vitamins, and supplements, before starting treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice any of the following after your injection: sudden vision changes or loss of vision, increased eye pain or significant eye discomfort, increased redness in the eye, sensitivity to light, seeing floaters (spots or threads in your vision), discharge coming from your eye, or swelling around the eye. These could be signs of a serious eye infection (endophthalmitis) or other complications that need immediate treatment. Also call your doctor if you have signs of a stroke or heart attack, such as sudden numbness or weakness on one side of your body, sudden trouble speaking, sudden severe headache, or chest pain.
when_it_works: Some patients notice improvement in their vision within the first few months of treatment, but results can vary. It may take several injections before you notice a difference. For many patients, the goal of treatment is to slow down or stop further vision loss rather than to fully restore vision. Be patient and continue with all scheduled appointments even if you do not notice immediate improvement. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular eye exams and imaging tests.
special_populations: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before starting this treatment. The effects of ranibizumab-eqrn on unborn babies or nursing infants are not fully known, so you and your doctor should carefully weigh the risks and benefits. If you have a history of stroke, heart attack, or other cardiovascular problems, make sure your doctor knows, as there may be a small risk of these events with this type of medicine. Older adults commonly use this medication for age-related macular degeneration and can generally receive it safely, but your doctor will monitor you closely.
